tool.name: FindRasterExtremeValues

summary.para:
View online help files: https://www.jennessent.com/topographic-analysis/find-raster-extreme-values.html
Finds the regional extremes of any raster surface -- on a DEM the peaks (summits) and low points (sinks); on a slope raster the steepest and flattest points; on a habitat-suitability surface the locations of best and worst habitat -- and writes one point per extreme, with the cell value, coordinates, prominence (topographic prominence / depression depth on a DEM; how far the value stands out from its surroundings on any other surface), and a flag for extremes on the edge of the data. Flat tops and flat-bottomed basins yield one point each; flats that drain are excluded. Honors the Output Coordinates environment. Needs no Spatial Analyst.

tool.usage:
What this tool does. It scans a raster surface -- typically a DEM -- for the places where the terrain reaches a local extreme, and writes each one as a point. The two kinds of extreme are perfect mirror images. A low point is a cell, or a connected flat of equal cells, with no lower neighbor: water arriving there has no outflow direction. A peak is exactly the same thing on the upside-down surface: a cell or flat with no higher neighbor -- a summit. One definition therefore serves both, and the tool simply runs it twice, once on the surface and once on its negation.
Not just elevation. Nothing in the algorithm assumes the surface is terrain -- it only compares cell values -- so the tool is just as useful on any continuous raster, and the vocabulary simply translates. Run it on a slope raster and the "peaks" are the steepest points on the landscape while the "low points" are the flattest. Run it on a habitat-suitability surface and it pins the exact locations of the best and the worst habitat -- the cores of the strongest patches and the centers of the least suitable ground. Temperature, wetness, cost, density, probability: any modeled surface works the same way. The Prominence value generalizes too: it reports how far each extreme stands above (or below) its surroundings before the surface crosses back, in the raster's own units -- so on a suitability surface, a high-prominence maximum is a strong, distinct patch of good habitat rather than a bump on an already-good plateau, and the minimum-prominence filter separates genuinely distinctive spots from noise on any surface, not just terrain.
Why not flow accumulation. An earlier idea defined peaks as cells with flow accumulation of zero. That test describes every cell with no upslope contributor -- entire ridgelines, divide crests, and the upper edge of every slope, often a quarter of the raster -- rather than summits. The local-extreme definition used here finds the summits themselves.
Flats are grouped; benches are rejected. Integer DEMs are full of ties, so a mesa top or a flat-bottomed basin can be hundreds of connected equal cells. The tool groups each such region and writes one point, placed at the region cell nearest the region's centroid (so an L-shaped flat does not get a point hanging in space). A flat bench partway down a hillside -- equal cells whose rim leads downhill -- is not an extreme and is excluded: a region only counts when every known neighbor beyond it lies strictly on the wrong side.
Prominence and depth. Every point carries a Prominence value. The tool computes it by merging cells in elevation order: for low points, from the lowest cell upward, with everything outside the raster treated as lower than any cell. Each extreme starts its own group, and when two groups meet, the one whose extreme is the less extreme of the two is finished and measured to the level at which they met -- the saddle. For a low point the number is the depth of its own basin below the saddle where it joins a deeper basin, or below the spill point where it drains off the raster -- how much water it would take to overflow. For a peak, the same procedure runs on the inverted surface, from the summits downward, and the number is the summit's topographic prominence: the drop from the summit to the key saddle separating it from higher ground -- the standard mountaineering measure of whether a bump deserves to be called a mountain. Every extreme gets its own number: a subsidiary summit on the shoulder of a higher one has a small prominence, and a small pit inside a larger bowl a small depth. Extremes whose saddle path leaves the raster, or runs into NoData, get the drop their region had made by the time it reached the outside -- a lower bound on the true prominence, flagged EdgeOfData = 1; an extreme lying on the edge itself, or beside NoData, has made no drop and gets 0. Of two exactly equal extremes in one basin, one is measured to the saddle between them and the other carries the basin's full depth. The optional minimum prominence filter uses these values to screen out noise: at 0 every raw extreme is kept; at, say, 10 elevation units the thousands of one-cell bumps and pits a real DEM produces disappear and the genuine features remain. Note that any positive threshold removes extremes lying on the edge of the data or beside NoData, since their prominence is 0.
The edge-of-data flag. An extreme whose region reaches the raster edge or NoData before it meets higher (or deeper) ground has its prominence measured against the edge rather than real terrain -- the number is a lower bound; an extreme lying on the edge itself has unknown neighbors and gets 0. Rather than silently dropping these, the tool writes every point with an EdgeOfData field (1 = measured against the edge of the data or NoData, so the prominence is a lower bound; 0 = measured against real terrain) so you can screen them out with a definition query when you want only fully known extremes.
The dominance radius. A circular filter that does two things at once: it enforces a minimum separation between the reported points, and it drops the lesser of any two extremes closer together than the radius (typically a small bump or hollow beside a bigger feature). The circle is every cell whose center lies within the radius of the point's center, so a diagonal neighbor counts the same as a cardinal one at the same distance. The default radius of 1.5 cells takes in exactly the eight immediate neighbors (the diagonal ones sit 1.41 cells away), which every extreme already dominates, so every regional extreme is reported; a radius of exactly 1 would reach only the four cardinal neighbors and change nothing either. The filter starts to act at a radius of 2. A larger radius keeps only points that are the most extreme cell within their circle -- radius 10 keeps a peak only if nothing higher lies within 10 cells of it in any direction -- which is a quick way to thin dense terrain to its dominant features. Unlike the prominence filter it never measures HOW FAR a point stands above or below its surroundings. It composes with the prominence filter; prominence is usually the more meaningful of the two.
Coordinate systems. The output feature class is created in the DEM's coordinate system unless the Output Coordinates geoprocessing environment is set, in which case that environment is honored (most tools in this suite deliberately ignore environments; this one respects this one, by design). The X and Y attribute fields always report the point's coordinates in the output feature class's actual coordinate system, so the fields never disagree with the geometry. Points are placed at cell centers.
Fields. Type (Peak / Low Point, with coded-value definitions in the field metadata); SrcRaster and SrcPath (the source raster's name and workspace, so the points remain traceable); CellValue (the extreme cell's value, in the raster's own units -- elevation on a DEM, slope on a slope raster, and so on); Prominence (as above, raster units); EdgeOfData (1/0); X and Y. The algorithm compares elevations only, so it works identically on projected and geographic rasters.
Reference. Sinks and D8 drainage: O'Callaghan, J.F., and D.M. Mark. 1984, "The extraction of drainage networks from digital elevation data," Computer Vision, Graphics, and Image Processing 28:323-344 (https://doi.org/10.1016/S0734-189X(84)80011-0).

dialogReference.para: The single-band raster surface whose extremes are to be found. A DEM gives summits and sinks, but any continuous surface works, because the tool only compares cell values: a slope raster gives the steepest and flattest points, a habitat-suitability surface gives the locations of best and worst habitat, and temperature, wetness, cost, or probability surfaces behave the same way. NoData cells are ignored; extremes beside them are flagged in the EdgeOfData field because some of their neighbors are unknown.
Whether to find peaks (summits: no higher neighbor), low points (sinks: no lower neighbor, i.e. no outflow direction), or both. With both, the Type field distinguishes them in the single output.

The output points, one per extreme, in the DEM's coordinate system unless the Output Coordinates environment overrides it. A name is suggested from the input. Fields: Type, SrcRaster, SrcPath, Elevation, Prominence, EdgeOfData, X, Y -- each documented in the output's field metadata.

Keep only extremes whose prominence (peaks: drop to the key saddle) or depth (low points: depth below the spill point) is at least this many raster elevation units. The default 0 keeps every raw extreme; a modest positive value removes the one-cell noise a real DEM produces. Any positive value also removes extremes lying on the edge of the data or beside NoData, whose prominence is 0.

Keep only extremes that are the most extreme cell within a circle of this radius, in cells, centered on them (every cell whose center lies within the radius; diagonal and cardinal neighbors count alike). This enforces a minimum separation between reported points and drops the lesser of any two extremes closer together than the radius. The default 1.5 is the eight immediate neighbors (diagonals sit 1.41 cells away), which every extreme already dominates, so it reports every regional extreme; radii below 2 change nothing; 10 keeps a peak only if nothing higher lies within 10 cells of it in any direction. Composes with the Minimum prominence filter.

scriptExample.title: Find Raster Extreme Values example (stand-alone script)
scriptExample.para: All extremes; then only substantial ones (prominence at least 20 elevation units); then peaks alone, reprojected by the environment. extreme_type values are exactly: "Both (peaks and low points)", "Peaks (high points) only", "Low points only".
scriptExample.code:
import arcpy arcpy.ImportToolbox(r"C:\path\to\JennessEnterprisesTools.pyt") # your installed path is shown in this tool's run messages
# Every peak and low point, with prominence/depth and edge flags arcpy.jenness.FindRasterExtremeValues( "dem.tif", "Both (peaks and low points)", r"C:\data\out.gdb\dem_Extremes", 0, 1)
# Only the substantial features: prominence / depth of 20 units or more arcpy.jenness.FindRasterExtremeValues( "dem.tif", "Both (peaks and low points)", r"C:\data\out.gdb\dem_Big", 20, 1)
# Peaks only, output reprojected by the Output Coordinates environment arcpy.env.outputCoordinateSystem = arcpy.SpatialReference(4326) arcpy.jenness.FindRasterExtremeValues( "dem.tif", "Peaks (high points) only", r"C:\data\out.gdb\dem_Peaks", 0, 1) arcpy.env.outputCoordinateSystem = None

dataIdInfo.idCredit: Jeff Jenness, Jenness Enterprises (http://www.jennessent.com). Prominence and depression depth follow the key-saddle definition, computed by merging cells in elevation order; sink and drainage definitions after O'Callaghan and Mark (1984), Computer Vision, Graphics, and Image Processing 28:323-344.
